notes.short: God's regret and grief, told in human words
notes.about: Scripture tells of the LORD's regret and grief in human words, so that we can understand how God regards man's sin. The same Bible says He “is not a man, that He should change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29).

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: how God regards man's sin, told in human words

original.note: In Hebrew “regretted” is nacham, the word Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 use when they say God does not “change His mind”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Genesis 6:6 under Anthropopatheia, human feelings spoken of God. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) sees the pain of the divine love; Henry and Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) read it as said after the manner of men, Henry finding in it no uneasiness in God but His displeasure at sin. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say God does not change His mind.
notes.limit: The writers agree the words are a figure, but not on whether they tell of a real grief in God or of His displeasure at sin and a change in how He deals with men.

cites.quote: not that He has such feelings; but, in infinite condescension, He is thus spoken of in order to enable us to comprehend Him.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The repentance of God is an anthropomorphic expression for the pain of the divine love at the sin of man
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These are expressions after the manner of men, and must be understood so as not to reflect upon the honour of God's immutability or felicity. … This language does not imply any passion or uneasiness in God (nothing can create disturbance to the Eternal Mind), but it expresses his just and holy displeasure against sin and sinners
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: by language suited to our nature and experience, He is described as about to alter His visible procedure towards mankind
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Abel's blood is given a voice that cries to God
notes.about: Abel is dead and silent, yet his blood is given a voice that cries out to the LORD. The picture shows that the murder itself calls on God to judge, even when no one else accuses the killer.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me
figure.means: the murder itself, known to God, calling for His justice though Abel is silent and no one accuses Cain

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Personification, among inanimate things spoken of as persons. Henry says God speaks as if the blood were both witness and prosecutor, since His own knowledge testified and His justice demanded satisfaction. Calvin: even when the one wronged is silent, the wrong alone moves God to punish; Abel was speechless, but the voice of his blood was louder than any orator.

cites.quote: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” See under Heterosis. So in verse 11. The earth is represented as opening her mouth to receive the blood of Abel.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He speaks as if the blood itself were both witness and prosecutor, because God's own knowledge testified against him and God's own justice demanded satisfaction. … Though they hold their peace, their blood has a loud and constant cry, to which the ear of the righteous God is always open.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: yet even when he who is injured is silent the injuries themselves are alone sufficient to arouse God to inflict punishment. … Abel was speechless when his throat was being cut, or in whatever other manner he was losing his life; but after death the voice of his blood was more vehement than any eloquence of the orator.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The LORD “smelled” the aroma: He accepted it
notes.about: Scripture says the LORD smelled the aroma of Noah's offering, speaking of God in human terms. It means He accepted the offering and was pleased with it. Paul uses the same picture of Christ, who gave Himself “as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (Ephesians 5:2).

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: that the LORD accepted Noah's offering and was pleased with it

original.note: In Hebrew the verb and its noun share one root, so He smelled the smell; and the aroma is an aroma of rest.

notes.evidence: Bullinger finds Anthropopatheia here: the LORD accepted the sacrifice and was satisfied with the atonement. Calvin: Moses, as is his way, speaks of God in human terms for an untaught people; Noah's piety was the sweet odour. Henry: God was pleased with Noah's zeal as men are with sweet smells, and the offering pictured Christ's. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): He accepted the offerer's feelings.
notes.limit: The writers agree that the words mean God accepted the offering. They put the weight in different places: on Noah's piety and thanks, or on the atonement and the sacrifice of Christ that it pictured.

cites.at: Polyptoton, Verbs with cognate noun, p. 275
cites.quote: Lit., smelled the sweet smell, or the savour of rest: i.e., Jehovah accepted the sacrifice, and was satisfied with the atonement made by Noah. ... The figure of Anthrōpopatheia ... is involved.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Moses here, according to his manner, invests God with a human character for the purpose of accommodating himself to the capacity of an ignorant people. ... This piety breathed a good and sweet odour before God
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He was well pleased with Noah's pious zeal, and these hopeful beginnings of the new world, as men are with fragrant and agreeable smells ... Christ's sacrifice of himself, which was typified and represented by it, and which was indeed an offering of a sweet-smelling savour
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He graciously accepted the feelings of the offerer which rose to Him in the odour of the sacrificial flame.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The LORD “came down to see”: told in human terms
notes.about: The LORD, who sees all and needs no journey, is said to come down to see the city and tower, as a king goes to look before he judges. The words tell in human terms how God took notice of the builders and stepped in. Genesis 18:21 speaks of Sodom in the same way.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's taking notice of the builders and stepping in to judge them, told as a king who goes to look

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the coming down an anthropomorphic description of God stepping into the doings of men, not a visible descent. Henry calls it an expression after the manner of men; Calvin says it is spoken with reference to men, since God does not move from place to place; Payne Smith (Ellicott) calls the telling anthropological, the LORD as a king who goes to inspect the work.
notes.limit: The note does not say the LORD came here in any visible form; the writers read the words as a picture of His taking notice and stepping in.

cites.quote: Jehovah's “coming down” is not the same here as in ... viz., the descent from heaven of some visible symbol of His presence, but is an anthropomorphic description of God's interposition in the actions of men
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is an expression after the manner of men; he knew it as clearly and fully as men know that which they come to the place to view. Observe, 1. Before he gave judgment upon their cause, he enquired into it; for God is incontestably just and fair in all his proceedings against sin and sinners, and condemns none unheard.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The descent of God, which Moses here records, is spoken of in reference to men rather than to God; who, as we know, does not move from place to place. But he intimates that God gradually and as with a tardy step, appeared in the character of an Avenger.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The narrative is given in that simple anthropological manner usual in the Book of Genesis, which so clearly sets before us God’s loving care of man, and here and in Gen 18:21 the equity of Divine justice. For Jehovah is described as a mighty king, who, hearing in His upper and heavenly dwelling of man’s ambitious purpose, determines to go and inspect the work in person
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: God will “go down to see”: said in human terms
notes.about: The LORD, who knows all things, speaks as a judge who must go and look into a charge before he knows the facts. The words are put in human terms, to show that His judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah is just and never rash.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: I will go down to see
figure.means: God's searching out of the facts before He judges, told as a man goes to look and learn

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia, where knowing is spoken of God as though He learned what He did not know. Henry and Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) call the words language after the manner of men, showing that God's judgment is not rash; Calvin says Moses brings Him in speaking after the manner of men because His forbearance is beyond us.
notes.limit: The note does not make the LORD's appearing to Abraham in this chapter a figure; the figure is in His speaking as one who must go and see in order to know.

cites.quote: Human Actions are attributed to God. ... Knowing. Not actual knowledge as such, but the acquiring of knowledge as though before ignorant.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Not as if there were any thing concerning which God is in doubt, or in the dark; but he is pleased thus to express himself after the manner of men, [1.] To show the incontestable equity of all his judicial proceedings. Men are apt to suggest that his way is not equal; but let them know that his judgments are the result of an eternal counsel, and are never rash or sudden resolves.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: I will go down . . . and see--language used after the manner of men. These cities were to be made examples to all future ages of God's severity; and therefore ample proof given that the judgment was neither rash nor excessive
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: he commends the moderation of God, who does not immediately fulminate against the ungodly and pour out his vengeance upon them ... Since, however, such forbearance of God cannot be comprehended by us, Moses introduces Him as speaking according to the manner of men.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.about: The angel of the LORD calls Abraham's name twice in a row, just as Abraham takes the knife (verse 10). The doubled name draws special attention to Abraham and to a solemn moment. God calls Jacob, Moses and Samuel by name twice in the same way.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.means: a name called twice, drawing special attention to Abraham at a solemn moment

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis: when thus used, the figure calls special attention to the person and to a solemn moment of importance.

cites.quote: When thus used, the figure calls special attention to the occasion or to the person, and to some solemn moment of importance in the action, or of significance in the words.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “Now I know”: God speaks in human terms
notes.about: The angel of the LORD speaks here as God (“from me”). God knew Abraham's heart already. The words “now I know” speak of Him in human terms, so that we can understand, and mark the proof Abraham had just given that he feared God.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God, who knew already, speaking in human terms of the proof Abraham gave that he feared Him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia, God's knowing told as if He learned it: God knew already, but stoops to make Abraham understand. Calvin says God speaks after the manner of men, to suit our weakness, and that Moses means Abraham proved his fear of God. Henry takes the angel to be God Himself, who knew it before, but Abraham had now given memorable proof of it.

cites.quote: God, of course, knew it already; but, in wondrous condescension, He stoops to make Abraham understand.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Truly, by condescending to the manner of men, God here says that what he has proved by experiment, is now made known to himself. And he speaks thus with us, not according to his own infinite wisdom, but according to our infirmity. Moses, however, simply means that Abraham, by this very act, testified how reverently he feared God.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The angel of the Lord, that is, God himself, the eternal Word, the angel of the covenant ... Now know I that thou fearest God. God knew it before, but now Abraham had given a most memorable evidence of it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Side by side: she urges him, Joseph refuses
notes.about: The chapter sets Joseph beside his master’s wife. She urges him day after day; he refuses, naming his master’s trust and his God, and at last runs from her, leaving his cloak in her hand. Her lust and his faithfulness each show up the other.

sides.label: Refuses, fearing to sin against God
sides.words: So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?

sides.label: Urges him day after day
sides.words: Although Potiphar’s wife spoke to Joseph day after day

notes.evidence: Henry sets a shameful instance of immodesty in Joseph's mistress against an illustrious instance of virtue in Joseph, kept by the grace of God. Calvin: her filthiness shows the blind force of lust, while Joseph is set before us as an example of fidelity and self-control. Benson: Joseph feared God, while she was deaf to conscience and the fear of God.

cites.quote: A most shameful instance of impudence and immodesty in Joseph's mistress ... Here is a most illustrious instance of virtue and resolved chastity in Joseph, who, by the grace of God, was enabled to resist and overcome this temptation
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Now as this filthiness is a signal proof that carnal lust acts from blind and furious impulses; so, in the person of Joseph, an admirable example of fidelity and continence is set before us.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: But Joseph feared God; Joseph believed in a judgment to come. ... Finding her dead to all sense of shame, and deaf to the calls of duty, honour, conscience, and the fear of God, and that she was not to be reclaimed, he avoided her company
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Seasons and days named one by one, with “and”
notes.about: God promises that the seasons and the days will not cease while the earth lasts. Eight words are named in four pairs, and in Hebrew every word after the first begins with “and”, so each is weighed on its own, showing how complete the covenant is, how full the blessing and how sure the promise.

figure.name: Polysyndeton
figure.words: seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night
figure.means: each of the seasons and the days weighed on its own, showing how complete the covenant is, how full the blessing and how sure God's promise

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Polysyndeton: the four pairs, joined by and throughout, show how complete the covenant is, how full the blessing and how sure God's promise. The BSB keeps the and only inside each pair; the Hebrew has it between the pairs as well.

cites.quote: the completeness of the covenant and the fulness of the blessing, and the certainty of the Divine promise, is set forth in a double four-fold description
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” No
notes.about: The LORD answers Sarah's laughter with a question that needs no answer. Nothing is too difficult for Him, so a son for Sarah in her old age is not beyond His power. Jeremiah says it plainly: “Nothing is too difficult for You!”

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Is anything too difficult for the LORD?
figure.means: nothing is too difficult for the LORD, not even a son for Sarah in her old age

original.note: In Hebrew “too difficult” is pala, to be wonderful: nothing is too wonderful for the LORD.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Erotesis, a question whose answer is an emphatic no. Henry says nothing escapes God's notice or exceeds His power. Calvin reads it as a rebuke of Sarah for measuring God's power by her own sense. Clarke reads it as asking whether any miracle is too great for Him, and says Luke 1:37 takes up the Septuagint's words almost exactly, as a statement instead of a question.
notes.limit: Some also read it as asking whether anything is hidden from the LORD: not even Sarah's silent laughter was. Others keep to His power alone.

cites.quote: where the question is put in the affirmative, and the answer to be supplied by the mind is a very emphatic negative. ... “Is anything too hard for the Lord?” (Gen 18:14 ). No! there is nothing too hard for Him
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Here is a question asked which is enough to answer all the cavils of flesh and blood: Is any thing too hard for the Lord? (Heb. too wonderful), that is, (1.) Is any thing so secret as to escape his cognizance? No, not Sarah's laughing, though it was only within herself. Or, (2.) Is any thing so difficult as to exceed his power? No, not the giving of a child to Sarah in her old age.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: For there is no little weight in this sentence, ‘Can anything be wonderful with God?’ But the angel chides Sarah, because she limited the power of God within the bounds of her own sense. An antithesis is therefore implied between the immense power of God, and the contracted measure which Sarah imagined to herself, through her carnal reason.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: i.e., Can any thing be too great a miracle for him to effect? ... which St. Luke adopts almost literatim, only making it an affirmative position instead of a question ... It was to correct Sarah's unbelief, and to strengthen her faith, that God spoke these most important words
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: God's words break off at “and live forever”
notes.about: God's words stop after “and live forever...” and never say what He will do. The next verse finishes them with a deed: “the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden”. The unspoken end can be read as too dreadful to put into words.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.means: what God will do is left unsaid; the next verse shows it in deed, as He sends man out of the garden, away from the tree of life

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Aposiopesis (Sudden Silence), in threatening: what follows is left unsaid, as though too awful to think on, but includes driving man from the tree of life. James G. Murphy (Barnes' Notes) says the next verse completes it by an act. Calvin finds the sentence lacking and supplies that man be barred from the tree. Keil says the account passes from God's words to acts.
notes.limit: The writers agree that the words stop short and leave the end to be supplied; that the silence hides something too awful to say is one writer's reading.

cites.at: Aposiopesis, or Sudden-Silence: Anger and Threatening, p. 152
cites.quote: Here the exact consequences of eating of the tree of life in his fallen condition are left unrevealed, as though they were too awful to be contemplated: and the sudden silence leaves us in the darkness in which the Fall involved us. But we may at least understand that whatever might be involved in this unspoken threatening, it included this fact:- I will drive him away from the tree of life!
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: “Lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat and live forever.” This sentence is completed by an act, not a word, as we shall see in the next verse.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There is a defect in the sentence which I think ought to be thus supplied: ‘It now remains that in future, he be debarred from the fruit of the tree of life;’
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In order that, after the germ of death had penetrated into his nature along with sin, he might not “take also of the tree of life, and eat and live for ever ... God sent him forth from the garden of Eden.” With וישׁלּחהוּ (sent him forth) the narrative passes over from the words to the actions of God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Cain, then Abel, then Abel, then Cain
notes.about: The two brothers are named Cain, Abel, then Abel, Cain: the birth of Cain and his work at the ends, the birth of Abel and his work in the middle.

lines.words: she conceived and gave birth to Cain.
Later she gave birth to Cain’s brother Abel.
Now Abel was a keeper of sheep,
while Cain was a tiller of the soil.

notes.evidence: Boys sets out Genesis 4:1-5 as two instances and says that in each, Cain is in the outer members and Abel in the central ones. This is the first.

cites.quote: In each of the above instances, we have Cain in the extreme, and Abel in the central members.
cites.read: the 1824 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/tactica-sacra

notes.short: Two offerings, told Cain, Abel, then Abel, Cain
notes.about: Cain brings his offering, then Abel brings his. The answer of the LORD takes them in reverse: first Abel and his offering, then Cain and his offering. Cain stands at the ends, Abel in the middle.

lines.words: Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD,
while Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock.
And the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering,
but He had no regard for Cain and his offering.

notes.evidence: Boys sets out Genesis 4:1-5 as two instances and says that in each, Cain is in the outer members and Abel in the central ones. This is the second.

cites.quote: In each of the above instances, we have Cain in the extreme, and Abel in the central members.
cites.read: the 1824 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/tactica-sacra

notes.short: Nimrod's fame became a common saying
notes.about: The verse quotes a saying people already used: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.” His deeds made his name a byword, so that others could be likened to him. Some read his hunting as reaching to men as well, and verse 10 tells of the kingdom he founded.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD
figure.means: a common byword that likened a mighty man, as hunter or as ruler, to Nimrod

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Genesis 10:9 under Parœmia, sayings quoted as already in use. Henry says Nimrod became famous to a proverb; Calvin, that it became a proverb of the powerful and the violent, each another Nimrod; Keil (Keil and Delitzsch), that Nimrod's course of life gave occasion to the proverb; James G. Murphy (Barnes' Notes), that his fame in hunting became proverbial.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether the saying remembered his hunting of animals or his rise to rule over men by force.

cites.at: Parœmia; or, Proverb: quoted as being already in use as such, p. 756
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... wherefore it is said, ‘Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the Lord’
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Nimrod was a great hunter; with this he began, and for this became famous to a proverb. Every great hunter is, in remembrance of him, called a Nimrod.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Nimrod was so mighty and imperious that it would be proper to say of any powerful tyrant, that he is another Nimrod. Yet the version of Jerome is satisfactory, that thence it became a proverb concerning the powerful and the violent, that they were like Nimrod.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This course of life gave occasion to the proverb, "like Nimrod, a mighty hunter against the Lord," which immortalized not his skill in hunting beasts, but the success of his hunting of men in the establishment of an imperial kingdom by tyranny and power.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Hunting is a comprehensive term, indicating the taking of any species of animal, whether of the air, the sea, or the land. Nimrod's distinction in this respect was so great as to become proverbial.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Abraham calls himself “dust and ashes” before God
notes.about: Pleading for Sodom, Abraham calls himself “dust and ashes.” He was more than that, a man with a living soul, but he names only what is lowest in himself and sets it beside the greatness of the Lord he dares to speak to. By making himself small, he shows how great God is.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: Abraham's own lowliness, set beside the greatness of the Lord he is speaking to

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis: Abraham sets himself against the high and holy God and takes the lowest place. Calvin says he picks what is most contemptible in himself, though he had a living soul, to empty himself of all dignity. Henry sets God's greatness beside Abraham's meanness. Clarke sees his soul humbled before God, as high thoughts of self mean low thoughts of God's majesty.

cites.quote: he implies much more than he expresses. In calling himself “dust and ashes,” he contrasts himself with the high and holy God whom he is addressing, and takes the place of a man most vile and a creature most abject.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: For what is mortal man when compared with God? ... Abraham, indeed was not forgetful that he possessed a living soul; but he selects what was most contemptible, in order to empty himself of all dignity.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He speaks as one amazed at his own boldness, and the liberty God graciously allowed him, considering God's greatness—he is the Lord; and his own meanness—but dust and ashes.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: By these expressions he shows how deeply his soul was humbled in the presence of God. He who has high thoughts of himself must have low thoughts of the dignity of the Divine nature, of the majesty of God, and the sinfulness of sin.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A threat of death with its condition left unsaid
notes.about: God tells Abimelech, “You are as good as dead,” and stops short of saying on what terms. Verse 7 makes plain what was left unsaid: if he does not restore Sarah, he “will surely die”; if he returns her, Abraham will pray for him and he will live.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: You are as good as dead
figure.means: a threat whose condition is not spoken: unless he gives the woman back, as verse 7 makes plain

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Genesis 20:3 under Aposiopesis (Sudden Silence), in anger and threatening: the words if you do not restore her must be supplied, or that her husband would kill him, and he says verse 7 makes this clear. Genesis 20:7 states the condition.
notes.limit: The verse reads as a whole sentence; the break lies in the condition the threat leaves out, which verse 7 supplies. The unsaid words may also be read as a warning that her husband would kill him.

cites.at: Aposiopesis, or Sudden-Silence: Anger and Threatening, p. 152

notes.short: A saying born on the mountain of the LORD
notes.about: The LORD's providing on the mountain passed into a saying that people still repeated: “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.” Many read it as a word of hope, that when His people are most in need the LORD will see to it and come to help.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided
figure.means: when His people are most in need the LORD will see to it and come to help, as He did for Abraham and Isaac on that mountain

original.note: In Hebrew “Will Provide” and “will be provided” both come from ra'ah, to see; to see to a need is to provide for it.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia among proverbs first found in Scripture that passed into general use. Payne Smith (Ellicott) says a proverb arose from it: in man's need God will see to it and provide. Poole: still used as a proverb, of the LORD seen in greatest extremities. Benson calls it a proverb in frequent use: in His people's extremities the LORD will appear to provide.
notes.limit: The saying's last word can also be read as seen, the LORD appearing on His mountain; the writers weigh both, and one joins them: He will show Himself by providing. Two of the writers also see in it a pointer to Christ, manifested and offered in that place.

notes.short: Rebekah's cry of grief is left unfinished
notes.about: The children struggle within Rebekah, and she cries out, “Why is this happening to me?” Her words of grief are left unfinished. The LORD had answered the prayer for a child, yet she suffers so; she does not say the rest, but goes to inquire of the LORD.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: Why is this happening to me?
figure.means: the rest of her complaint, unsaid: if the prayer for a child was answered, why must she suffer so, and why did she wish for one?

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Aposiopesis, the sudden silence of grief and complaint: Rebekah's words are not completed, for she could not see why an answered prayer should bring such suffering. Clarke calls it an imperfect speech, born of her perplexity, and gives its sense: if she must suffer so, why did she ever wish for a child?
notes.limit: The two writers fill in her unspoken words a little differently.

cites.quote: Rebekah’s words of grief and complaint are not completed. She could not understand why, if Jehovah was intreated and answered Isaac’s prayer, she should so suffer that the answer was almost as hard to be borne as her former condition.

cites.quote: It appears she was in considerable perplexity, hence that imperfect speech, If so, why am I thus? the simple meaning of which is probably this; if I must suffer such things, why did I ever wish to have a child?

original.note: In Hebrew her words begin with “if so” and run: if so, why this, I? She does not complete the sentence.

notes.short: “Shiloh,” a dark name for the coming King
notes.about: Jacob says the scepter will stay with Judah until Shiloh comes. The name is dark and its exact meaning is debated, but it is read as a name of the Messiah, the King from Judah to whom the nations will give their allegiance.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.means: the Messiah, the King to come from Judah, whom the nations will obey

original.note: In Hebrew Shiloh is elsewhere the name of a town; here it can be read as the name of a person, the bearer of rest.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ænigma, a dark saying. Calvin calls the passage obscure but certain to promise the Messiah from Judah. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls Shiloh an obscure word, explained in several ways, meaning the Messiah. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) takes it as a title of the Messiah, the bearer of rest, though the grammar of the word may be uncertain.
notes.limit: The writers explain the word itself in different ways, such as the one sent, the seed or the bearer of rest; those who explain it agree that it points to the Messiah.

cites.quote: is in the form of Enigma. “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” See under Metonymy.
